source.title: Llasa: Scaling Train-Time and Inference-Time Compute for Llama-based Speech Synthesis
source.authors: Zhen Ye; Xin-Fa Zhu; Chi-Min Chan; Xin-Sheng Wang; Xu Tan; Jia-He Lei; Yi Peng; Haohe Liu; Yizhu Jin; Zhe-Qi Dai; Hongzhan Lin; Jianyi Chen; Xing-Jian Du; Liu-Meng Xue; Yun-Lin Chen; Zhi-Fei Li; Lei Xie; Qiu-Qiang Kong; Yi-Ke Guo; Wei Xue

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how speech-synthesis outcomes vary with model size and training-data scale, using speech-quality and synthesis-task metrics rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy or power-law fits.
record.gate_note: The paper reports speech synthesis outcomes across model sizes and training-data amounts, which bear on V6. It does not report held-out pretraining loss, power-law fits or exponents, small-run extrapolation, or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its speech scaling results therefore do not test V1–V5 or V7 as specified. Codec comparisons and inference-time search comparisons are not rows here because they do not test the claim versions' scale relationship.
record.test_reason: Llasa is a Llama-initialised speech-token LM. Its TTS metrics are tracked at three model sizes (1B/3B/8B at 250k h) and three data sizes (80k/160k/250k h at 1B). This bears only on the directional part of V6 (task performance improves with scale) in a new setting. No loss, power-law fit or prediction is reported, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested, and so is V6's 'predictably'. These are the model's trained task metrics, not downstream tasks of a separately pretrained model, so the V6 link is loose.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that larger models and more data improve naturalness, prosody and text comprehension, and that verifier-guided inference-time search improves similarity, emotion and accuracy. They call the train-time gains 'consistent', although their own tables show non-monotonic cases (3B test-hard WER, 8B continuation SIM). They fit no scaling law and say they do not seek a compute-optimal configuration.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales a speech-synthesis system and evaluates speech-generation outcomes; it does not use the original studies' held-out language-model loss measurement, power-law fitting, or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported task gains vary by metric and category: some tasks show only marginal improvement, rare characters benefit mainly from data coverage, and English Compound Nouns and Foreign Words primarily benefit from increased data rather than model scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Inference-time search (PRM/ORM with verifiers) lets smaller Llasa models approach or match larger ones. Larger models generally benefit more from search.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In TTS, inference-time compute can substitute partly for train-time model scale.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the relevant scaling results. The sweeps use a limited set of discrete model sizes and data amounts, and the paper does not fit a scaling curve or test prediction from smaller runs. Figure 1's expert-score values are not legible as numbers in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted other Table 2 test-set metrics and Table 2/3 inference-time-search rows to stay focused on train-time scaling outcomes relevant to V6; omitted individual category-level Figure 1 values because the supplied text gives no numeric values. Table 2/3/4 and Figure 1 are the locations.

untested.parts: Whether task gains are predictable: no fitted curve, no prediction of larger runs, no relation to pretraining loss. Only three discrete points per axis, with no uncertainty.
No held-out loss versus parameters, data or compute.
No small-run fit and no extrapolation.
The authors state they do not seek a compute-optimal configuration.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Speech modality, but no power-law form is fitted or tested.
No exponents or fitting choices compared.

record.verdict_notes: Train-time results for test-zh (CER 2.69→1.59, monotone) and test-en (WER 3.71→2.97; SIM-o dips at 8B, 0.579→0.574) are in Table 2. rows_left_out declares them, but they would strengthen both labels. The fits_no_version entry has no rows because rows_left_out declares the inference-time rows. Model sizes come from different Llama versions (3.2 for 1B/3B, 3.1 for 8B), and all runs train 3 epochs, so compute is not held fixed. The 80k/160k sets are random subsets of the 250k set.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy or loss-versus-parameter, token, or compute power-law measurement.
No power-law fit on smaller runs or extrapolation test on larger runs.
The paper says its goal is not to find a compute-optimal TTS configuration; it does not compare parameter/token allocations at fixed compute or fit their trends.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
Although it studies speech synthesis, it does not test whether the same power-law form holds in this modality or fit such a form.
Measures synthesis-task outcomes across selected model/data scales, but does not test whether those outcomes can be predicted from pretraining loss or a fitted scaling curve.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents, parameter-counting methods, or curve bending away from a power law.

relationships.condition: Data scaling at 1B (80k→160k→250k h) and model scaling to 8B on emotion similarity and the test-hard metrics
relationships.reason: Emotion similarity rises monotonically in both languages (R12, R13, R15, R17–R20). Test-hard WER/SIM improve at 250k and at 8B (R3, R5). Expert scores rise on emotion, poetry and tongue twisters (R22). Improvement is shown, not predictability.
relationships.display_finding: Emotion similarity increased at every data step in both languages, test-hard WER and similarity improved at 250k hours and 8B, and expert ratings increased for emotion, poetry and tongue twisters.

relationships.condition: Model-size scaling on some metrics; some task categories
relationships.reason: Test-hard WER is worse at 3B than 1B (R4). Continuation SIM is flat or slightly down at 8B (R10). Gains are negligible from 160k→250k on continuation and from 1B→3B on English emotion (R8, R9, R14). Questions gain marginally (R21). Rare characters, compound nouns and foreign words gain from data but little from model size (R23, R24).
relationships.display_finding: Test-hard WER worsened from 1B to 3B, continuation similarity stalled or declined at 8B, gains were negligible from 160k to 250k for continuation and 1B to 3B for English emotion, questions improved marginally, and rare characters, compound nouns, and foreign words benefited more from data than model size.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Across the reported speech-synthesis metrics and task settings where scores rise with more data or model size
reader_labels.reason: The tables and text report improvements in many synthesis outcomes across the training-data and model-size sweeps (R2–R3, R5, R7–R9, R12–R15, R17–R20, R22).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Metrics and task categories with weak, non-monotonic, or scale-specific gains
reader_labels.reason: The 3B test-hard WER is worse than the 1B value at 250k hours, the continuation SIM metrics dip slightly at 8B, and some text categories benefit more from data than model size or show only marginal gains (R4, R10, R21, R23, R24).
